rounds.response:
Goal: test how different online-homework feedback types affect undergraduates’ adaptation of study strategies, performance, and equity-related outcomes in intro psych courses.  
Key research questions: (1) Do feedback types (corrective feedback only vs. corrective + metacognitive prompts vs. corrective + concrete strategy suggestions) produce different trajectories of self-regulated learning (SRL) behaviors across a semester? (2) How do changes in SRL mediate performance gains (homework accuracy, exam scores) and course retention? (3) Do effects differ by equity-relevant student characteristics (first-generation status, URM, incoming GPA)?  
Two plausible designs: A) randomized-within-course (randomize students or assignments to feedback conditions; collect homework/LMS logs, pre/post SRL questionnaires, weekly short strategy reports, and a small think-aloud subsample); B) quasi-experimental across semesters (baseline semester observation, then implement one feedback intervention in next semester) with the same outcome measures—both designs require power checks and a planned subsample for process interviews.  
6–9 month milestone plan: months 0–2 finalize RQs/measures, secure instructor buy-in, and submit IRB; months 2–4 build feedback workflows in the homework system and pilot with ~20 students; months 4–8 run the semester study and monitor data quality; months 8–9 de-identify data per SOPs, run primary analyses, and draft internal report/seed-grant deliverables.  
Next steps: confirm PI/instructor support and which design they prefer, then I’ll draft the IRB application, measurement instruments, and a task list with responsible team members and estimated budget items.

rounds.response:
Background and Motivation: Building on our lab’s prior work linking student motivation and learning-analytics indicators in introductory courses, this project examines how undergraduates adapt self-regulated learning (SRL) strategies in response to different kinds of automated feedback from an online homework system, leveraging our existing LMS integrations, validated SRL measures, and the lab’s IRB/data-management SOPs.  
Research Questions: 1) Do different feedback types (corrective-only vs corrective+metacognitive prompts vs corrective+concrete strategy suggestions) produce different trajectories of students’ SRL behaviors across a semester; 2) To what extent do changes in SRL mediate course performance outcomes (homework accuracy, exam scores, course retention); 3) Do effects differ by equity-relevant characteristics (first-generation status, URM status, incoming GPA).  
Study Design and Data Plan — Primary design: a within-course randomized trial (randomize students or assignments to feedback conditions) collecting LMS/homework logs, pre/post validated SRL questionnaires, weekly brief strategy self-reports, and a think-aloud/process-interview subsample; primary outcomes = homework accuracy, exam scores, and retention; all data handling will follow IRB approval and lab SOPs.  
Study Design and Data Plan — Alternative design: a quasi-experimental across-semesters approach (baseline semester observation, then implement one intervention semester) with matched instructor/course controls and the same measures, using covariate adjustment or propensity methods to address nonrandom assignment.  
Timeline and Feasibility — Milestones (6–9 months):  
- Months 0–2: finalize RQs/measures, secure instructor buy-in, prepare and submit IRB per lab SOPs.  
- Months 2–4: develop feedback workflows in the homework system, implement logging, and pilot with ~20 students to test usability and data pipelines.  
- Months 4–8: run main semester study, monitor data quality and participant compliance, conduct interim checks.  
- Months 8–9: de-identify and store data per SOPs, run primary analyses, and draft the internal concept-note/report for the seed-grant submission.

Background and Motivation: Building on our lab’s prior work linking student motivation and learning-analytics indicators in introductory psychology courses, this project will examine how undergraduates adapt self-regulated learning (SRL) strategies in response to different automated feedback types from an online homework system, leveraging our existing LMS integrations, validated SRL measures, and the lab’s IRB and data-management SOPs to inform scalable, equity-minded instructional improvements.  
Research Questions: 1) Do different feedback types (corrective-only vs corrective + metacognitive prompts vs corrective + concrete strategy suggestions) produce different trajectories of students’ SRL behaviors across a semester; 2) To what extent do changes in SRL mediate course performance outcomes (homework accuracy, exam scores, course retention); 3) Do effects differ by equity-relevant characteristics (first-generation status, URM status, incoming GPA).  
Study Design and Data Plan: Primary design is a within-course randomized trial (randomize students or assignments to feedback conditions) collecting LMS/homework logs, pre/post validated SRL questionnaires, weekly brief strategy self-reports, and a think-aloud/process-interview subsample; primary outcomes are homework accuracy, exam scores, and retention, and all data collection, de-identification, and storage will follow IRB approval and lab SOPs.  
Study Design and Data Plan (alternative): The backup approach is a quasi-experimental across-semesters design (baseline semester observation followed by an intervention semester) with matched instructor/course controls and covariate adjustment or propensity methods to address nonrandom assignment while using the same measures and data-governance procedures.  
Timeline and Feasibility: Months 0–2 finalize RQs/measures, secure instructor buy-in, and prepare/submit IRB per SOPs; months 2–4 develop feedback workflows in the homework system, implement logging, and pilot with ~20 students to test usability and data pipelines; months 4–8 run the main semester study, monitor data quality and participant compliance, and conduct interim checks; months 8–9 de-identify and store data per SOPs, run primary analyses, and draft the internal concept-note/report for the seed-grant submission, a schedule we view as feasible given existing technical integrations and instructor partnerships.
